verdict.reasoning: Patient says symptoms started "about two to three days ago" and describes being "short of breath" with running and brisk walking, plus "just wheezing a bit, and coughing and just generally a bit short of breath."
Patient: "about two to three days ago, I was running with a friend... I found myself actually short of breath" and later "definitely um, if I'm walking briskly now."
Patient: "I've used my blue inhaler but to no avail. It hasn't really helped me."
When asked about phlegm, patient says "no I don't" and doctor summarizes "OK, no sputum, OK."
Doctor: "have you ever been admitted in hospital because your was so bad?" Patient: "no, I haven't." Also: "When was the last time you had an asthma attack?" Patient: "about three to four years ago."
Doctor: "have you ever had oral steroids in the past?" Patient: "no." Doctor: "When was the last time you had an asthma review with our nurse?" Patient: "about two years ago."

Doctor: "So, what was what's your peak flow reading when you're good?" then suggests "it's about, um, three eighty" and patient agrees "Yeah." Patient also says: "I haven't done overlap since I've has symptoms" indicating not checked since onset.
The entire consultation is about asthma; doctor refers to "your asthma" being under control and mentions "asthma attack" and "asthma check," implying established asthma history.

Patient: "I've used my blue inhaler" and "I think I'm just using that as and when I have symptoms"; doctor asks if using it every day and patient: "yeah, and morning or evening to kinda prevent it as well."

Patient: "I think I'm using that every day" in response to preventer use, and doctor clarifies dosing: "So, how are you using the ? Is it twice a day?" Patient: "Um, yes." Later doctor refers to "the brown your Clenil... you can increase it to four puffs twice a day," confirming a brown preventer inhaler (Clenil) used twice daily.
Patient: "Cetraben and Hydrocortisone."
Patient lists "Hydrocortisone" among current medications: "Cetraben and Hydrocortisone."
Patient: "I have hay fever." Doctor then asks: "any allergies to medication?" Patient: "Ohh no" and doctor concludes: "So you're not allergic to anything? OK. So no allergies." (no drug allergies).
Patient: "my brother is asthmatic and my sister has eczema."
Doctor: "it looks like you can be having a small, small exacerbation" and both note symptoms have worsened "in the last two to three days." This supports mild exacerbation/poor control over 2–3 days.
Patient has hay fever (an atopic condition) and uses Cetraben and Hydrocortisone with "a few issues... that I think could be eczema as well." Family history of eczema also supports atopy.
Doctor: "the brown your Clenil. The brown inhaler... If you're using just three puffs twice a day, you can increase it to four puffs twice a day... while you're waiting to see us."
Doctor: "you can use your blue inhaler as and when... You can use it maximum about every two to four, four hours" and later reiterates "salbutamol inhalers up to every two hourly."

Doctor: "I would like you to be seen by one of our GP's in the next few days" and later "I will recommend that meet her face to face." Also: "we're gonna examine your chest... Make you do the peak flow reading."
Doctor: "depending on what we find, you might need some antibiotics and some steroids." (oral corticosteroids are the implied form in this context).

Doctor: "if you're using [blue inhaler] that often... your asthma is really bad" and "if your breathing is getting really worse, then you would need to take yourself to A and E... if you breathing's getting worse and you've not seen us, do take your puffs to A and E."
